All emotions are normal; the behavior that follows can be healthy or unhealthy
quiz.e: All emotions are valid signals; it's the resulting behavior that can be constructive or harmful.

quiz.q: What role does sleep play in mental health?
o: It has no connection to mental health
Poor sleep is linked to worse mood regulation and higher stress
quiz.e: Sleep quality strongly affects mood regulation, stress levels, and overall mental health.

quiz.q: Which best explains why mental illness is not a 'choice'?
o: It involves real changes in brain chemistry, genetics, and environmental factors
People choose to feel sad on purpose
It is entirely controllable by willpower
It only affects people who want attention
quiz.e: Mental illness has biological and environmental roots, just like physical illness — it is not a choice.

quiz.q: Which macronutrient is the body's primary and preferred energy source?
quiz.e: Carbohydrates are broken down into glucose, the body's preferred fuel source.

quiz.q: How many calories does one gram of fat provide?
quiz.e: Fat provides about 9 calories per gram, more than double carbs or protein.

quiz.q: Which food group provides amino acids for building and repairing tissue?
quiz.e: Proteins are made of amino acids that build and repair body tissue, including muscle.

quiz.q: Complex carbohydrates differ from simple carbohydrates in that they:
o: Digest quickly and spike blood sugar
Digest slowly and provide steady energy
quiz.e: Complex carbs (whole grains, vegetables) digest slowly, providing sustained energy.

quiz.q: Which type of fat is linked to improved heart health?
quiz.e: Unsaturated fats, found in olive oil, nuts, and fish, support cardiovascular health.

quiz.q: Vitamin D works with which mineral to build strong bones?
quiz.e: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, essential for bone strength.

quiz.q: Iron deficiency in the diet most directly leads to:
quiz.e: Iron carries oxygen in the blood; too little causes anemia, resulting in fatigue and weakness.

quiz.q: According to MyPlate, what portion of the plate should be fruits and vegetables?
quiz.e: MyPlate recommends filling half the plate with fruits and vegetables.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a whole grain?
quiz.e: Brown rice retains its bran and germ, making it a whole grain with more fiber and nutrients.

quiz.q: On a nutrition label, which item helps you judge how many calories you're actually eating?
quiz.e: Serving size determines how the listed calories and nutrients apply to what you actually eat.

quiz.q: Cardiorespiratory endurance refers to:
o: The maximum weight a muscle can lift once
The heart and lungs' ability to supply oxygen during sustained activity
The range of motion at a joint
The ratio of fat to lean body mass
quiz.e: Cardiorespiratory endurance measures how well the heart and lungs sustain activity over time.

quiz.q: Doing many push-ups without stopping primarily demonstrates:
quiz.e: Muscular endurance is a muscle's ability to perform repeated contractions without fatigue.

quiz.q: What does the 'F' in the FITT principle stand for?
quiz.e: FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type — a framework for designing exercise plans.

quiz.q: How many minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity does the CDC recommend daily for teens?
quiz.e: The CDC recommends teens get at least 60 minutes of physical activity daily.

quiz.q: Endorphins released during exercise primarily help with:
quiz.e: Exercise releases endorphins, which improve mood and reduce stress and anxiety.

quiz.q: Which component of fitness is improved through regular stretching?
quiz.e: Flexibility is the range of motion at a joint, improved by stretching.

quiz.q: Anorexia nervosa is best described as:
o: Severe food restriction driven by intense fear of weight gain and distorted body image
A normal part of teen development
quiz.e: Anorexia involves dangerous food restriction rooted in fear of weight gain and body image distortion.

quiz.q: Bulimia nervosa involves cycles of:
o: Binge eating followed by purging behaviors
quiz.e: Bulimia is characterized by binge eating followed by compensatory purging behaviors.

quiz.q: Binge eating disorder differs from bulimia because it:
o: Does not involve purging after binge episodes
Is not a real medical condition
quiz.e: Binge eating disorder involves loss-of-control eating episodes without compensatory purging.

quiz.q: Which statement about eating disorders is accurate?
o: They are simply about wanting to look good
They are serious mental illnesses with biological, psychological, and social causes
quiz.e: Eating disorders are complex mental illnesses requiring professional treatment, not lifestyle choices.

quiz.q: Which is the healthiest approach to weight management?
o: Balanced nutrition and regular physical activity
Eliminating entire food groups without medical guidance
quiz.e: Sustainable weight management relies on balanced eating and consistent activity, not extreme measures.

quiz.q: Water-soluble vitamins like vitamin C are unique because they:
o: Are stored long-term in body fat
Are not stored well and need regular replenishment
quiz.e: Water-soluble vitamins aren't stored well by the body and must be consumed regularly.

quiz.q: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed with the help of:
quiz.e: Fat-soluble vitamins require dietary fat for proper absorption in the body.

quiz.q: Muscular strength is best demonstrated by:
o: Lifting the maximum weight possible in a single effort
Having a low body fat percentage
quiz.e: Muscular strength is the maximum force a muscle can generate in one effort.

quiz.q: Body composition refers to:
o: The ratio of fat mass to lean mass in the body
quiz.e: Body composition compares fat mass to lean mass (muscle, bone, organs).

quiz.q: Which is a reason media images can distort body image?
o: They are always unedited and accurate
They are often filtered or edited, creating unrealistic standards
They show only healthy body types
They have no influence on self-perception
quiz.e: Edited media images often present unattainable standards that distort perceptions of normal bodies.

quiz.q: Which snack best reflects a balanced, nutrient-dense choice?
quiz.e: Apple slices with peanut butter provide fiber, protein, and healthy fat in a balanced snack.

quiz.q: Why is portion control important even when eating healthy foods?
o: Overeating even healthy foods can lead to excess calorie intake and weight gain
Portion size doesn't affect calorie intake
Only unhealthy foods need portion control
quiz.e: Calories add up regardless of food quality, so portion size still matters for weight management.

quiz.q: Which activity best builds cardiorespiratory endurance?
o: Running or swimming for a sustained period
quiz.e: Sustained aerobic activities like running or swimming build cardiorespiratory endurance.

quiz.q: Resistance/strength training is especially important during adolescence because it:
o: Has no effect on developing bodies
Builds muscle and bone density during a key growth period
quiz.e: Strength training supports healthy bone density development during teen growth years.

quiz.q: Which best explains why skipping breakfast can backfire for weight management?
o: It has no effect on hunger later
It can lead to overeating later in the day
quiz.e: Skipping meals often leads to greater hunger and overeating later, undermining weight goals.

quiz.q: Added sugars on a nutrition label are important to check because:
o: Excess added sugar intake is linked to weight gain and other health issues
They are required for good health
quiz.e: High added sugar intake is linked to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other health problems.

quiz.q: Which best describes a balanced weekly exercise plan?
o: A mix of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities
quiz.e: A well-rounded plan includes both aerobic exercise and muscle-strengthening activities.

quiz.q: Sodium intake that is consistently too high is most associated with:
o: Increased risk of high blood pressure
quiz.e: Excess sodium intake is linked to higher blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.

quiz.q: Which best reflects the purpose of the MyPlate model compared to the older food pyramid?
o: It gives a simple visual for balanced portions across food groups
It eliminates the need for vegetables
quiz.e: MyPlate visually simplifies balanced portioning across the major food groups.

quiz.q: Lean protein sources recommended by MyPlate include:
o: Poultry, fish, beans, eggs, and nuts
quiz.e: MyPlate recommends lean proteins such as poultry, fish, beans, eggs, and nuts.

quiz.q: A person with binge eating disorder experiences which key feeling during an episode?
o: A loss of control over eating large amounts of food
quiz.e: A hallmark of binge eating disorder is a felt loss of control during eating episodes.

quiz.q: Which best supports recovery from an eating disorder?
o: Professional treatment involving medical and mental health support
Ignoring the behavior until it stops
quiz.e: Eating disorders require professional medical and mental health treatment for safe recovery.

quiz.q: B vitamins primarily help the body:
o: Convert food into usable energy at the cellular level
quiz.e: B vitamins play a key role in metabolizing food into usable cellular energy.

quiz.q: Which best summarizes a healthy overall approach to nutrition and fitness?
o: Extreme diets combined with excessive exercise
A varied, balanced diet paired with regular, well-rounded physical activity
Exercising only when trying to lose weight
quiz.e: Balanced nutrition and consistent, varied physical activity together support long-term health.

quiz.q: Which category of drugs slows down central nervous system activity?
quiz.e: Depressants like alcohol and opioids slow CNS activity, causing relaxation and slowed breathing.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a stimulant?
quiz.e: Nicotine speeds up the central nervous system, increasing heart rate and alertness.

quiz.q: Hallucinogens primarily affect the body by:
o: Slowing heart rate to dangerous levels only
quiz.e: Hallucinogens like LSD distort sensory perception and thought patterns.

quiz.q: Tolerance is best defined as:
o: Needing more of a substance over time for the same effect
A substance with no addictive potential
quiz.e: Tolerance means the body requires increasing amounts to achieve the same effect.

quiz.q: Physical dependence occurs when:
o: A person enjoys a substance occasionally
The body adapts to a substance and experiences withdrawal without it
A person tries a substance once
A substance has no chemical effect
quiz.e: Physical dependence means the body has adapted and withdrawal occurs without continued use.

quiz.q: Which body system does alcohol impair first, affecting judgment?
quiz.e: Alcohol impairs the frontal lobe first, affecting judgment before physical coordination.

quiz.q: Binge drinking for males is generally defined as:
o: 5 or more drinks in about two hours
quiz.e: Binge drinking for males is 5+ drinks within about a two-hour period.

quiz.q: Signs of alcohol poisoning include:
quiz.e: Alcohol poisoning is a medical emergency marked by vomiting, unconsciousness, and slowed breathing.

quiz.q: Why is the teen brain more vulnerable to alcohol's effects?
o: The prefrontal cortex is still developing until the mid-20s
Teens process alcohol faster than adults
Teen brains are fully developed by age 12
Alcohol has no effect on developing brains
quiz.e: The prefrontal cortex, responsible for judgment, isn't fully developed until the mid-20s, increasing vulnerability.

quiz.q: Long-term heavy alcohol use is most linked to:
quiz.e: Chronic heavy drinking damages the liver and raises cancer risk.

quiz.q: How quickly does nicotine reach the brain after inhalation?
quiz.e: Nicotine reaches the brain within seconds, quickly creating dependence.

quiz.q: Which statement about vaping is accurate?
o: It delivers addictive nicotine and heated chemicals, and is not a proven-safe alternative
It is only used by adults
quiz.e: Vaping delivers nicotine and other chemicals and carries real health risks despite marketing claims.

quiz.q: Tobacco use is considered:
o: The leading preventable cause of death in the U.S.
quiz.e: Long-term tobacco use is the leading preventable cause of death in the United States.

quiz.q: Nicotine exposure during adolescence can affect brain development related to:
quiz.e: Adolescent nicotine exposure can impair brain development tied to attention and impulse control.

quiz.q: Secondhand smoke exposure means:
o: Only smokers are affected by tobacco's chemicals
Non-smokers nearby are also exposed to many harmful chemicals
It has no effect on bystanders
quiz.e: Secondhand smoke exposes nearby non-smokers to many of the same harmful chemicals.

quiz.q: THC is the main psychoactive compound found in:
quiz.e: THC is the primary compound in marijuana responsible for its psychoactive effects.

quiz.q: Regular marijuana use during adolescence is linked to:
o: Impaired memory and learning due to ongoing brain development
quiz.e: Because the teen brain is still developing, regular use is linked to memory and learning impairment.

quiz.q: Opioids are dangerous in overdose primarily because they can cause:
quiz.e: Opioid overdose can suppress breathing to a fatal degree, called respiratory depression.

quiz.q: Fentanyl is dangerous because it:
o: Is rarely found in other drugs
Is a powerful synthetic opioid increasingly mixed into other drugs, raising overdose risk
Has no effect on the body
quiz.e: Fentanyl's potency, even in small amounts, dramatically raises overdose risk when mixed into other drugs.

quiz.q: Naloxone (Narcan) is used to:
quiz.e: Naloxone can rapidly reverse the effects of an opioid overdose if given in time.

quiz.q: Prescription drug misuse refers to:
o: Taking medication not prescribed to you, or more than prescribed
quiz.e: Misuse includes taking someone else's prescription or exceeding the prescribed dose.

quiz.q: Which is a protective factor against substance use?
o: Strong family bonds and clear expectations
quiz.e: Strong family bonds and clear expectations are well-documented protective factors.

quiz.q: Indirect peer pressure occurs when a person:
o: Is directly told to use a substance
Feels pressure to fit in without being explicitly asked
quiz.e: Indirect peer pressure comes from the desire to fit in, without explicit urging.

quiz.q: Which is an effective refusal skill?
o: Avoiding eye contact and saying nothing
Clearly saying no, offering an alternative, and being ready to leave
Pretending you don't hear the request
quiz.e: Clear refusal, an alternative suggestion, and willingness to leave are effective refusal strategies.

quiz.q: How can media and advertising influence substance use?
o: They have no influence on behavior
They can normalize substance use through appealing imagery
quiz.e: Advertising can make substances seem appealing or normal, influencing attitudes and behavior.

quiz.q: Early use of any addictive substance is linked to:
o: Increased statistical risk of developing dependence later in life
quiz.e: Starting substance use earlier in life is linked to higher risk of later dependence.

quiz.q: Addiction is best classified medically as:
o: A personal choice with no biological basis
A chronic brain disease affecting the reward system
A temporary phase with no lasting effects
quiz.e: Addiction is recognized as a chronic disease altering brain chemistry, particularly dopamine pathways.

quiz.q: Withdrawal symptoms occur when:
o: A person tries a substance for the first time
A physically dependent person stops using a substance
A person has never used a substance
quiz.e: Withdrawal happens when a dependent person's body reacts to the absence of the substance.

quiz.q: Which combination often makes up effective addiction treatment?
o: Behavioral therapy, support groups, and sometimes medication-assisted treatment
quiz.e: Comprehensive treatment often combines therapy, support groups, and medication when appropriate.

quiz.q: Relapse during recovery from addiction means:
o: Treatment has completely failed and should stop
It often signals a need to adjust the treatment plan, not a failure of the person
quiz.e: Relapse is common in chronic disease management and signals a need to adjust treatment, not failure.

quiz.q: Supportive, non-judgmental relationships during recovery:
o: Significantly improve the likelihood of successful long-term recovery
quiz.e: Strong social support is strongly associated with better long-term recovery outcomes.

quiz.q: Which best defines blood alcohol concentration (BAC)?
o: The percentage of alcohol in the bloodstream
The number of drinks consumed in a lifetime
quiz.e: BAC measures the percentage of alcohol present in a person's bloodstream.

quiz.q: Which factor affects how quickly BAC rises?
o: Body weight, sex, and speed of alcohol consumption
quiz.e: BAC is influenced by body weight, biological sex, and how fast alcohol is consumed.

quiz.q: Cigarette smoke contains which harmful gas, also found in car exhaust?
quiz.e: Cigarette smoke contains carbon monoxide, which reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.

quiz.q: Which is a documented long-term effect of tobacco use?
o: Increased risk of lung cancer, heart disease, and COPD
quiz.e: Long-term tobacco use significantly raises risk for lung cancer, heart disease, and COPD.

quiz.q: Which best explains why prevention programs teach refusal skills?
o: To help people avoid all social situations
To reduce the likelihood of giving in to peer pressure to use substances
Refusal skills have no proven benefit
quiz.e: Refusal skills are a core prevention strategy shown to reduce substance use initiation.

quiz.q: Which statement about opioid overdose risk is accurate?
o: Overdose risk is eliminated when opioids are mixed with fentanyl
Fentanyl contamination in other drugs greatly increases overdose risk, even unknowingly
Only heroin users are at risk of opioid overdose
Prescription opioids carry no overdose risk
quiz.e: Fentanyl is often mixed into other drugs without the user's knowledge, dramatically raising overdose risk.

quiz.q: Which best describes the relationship between stress and substance use risk?
o: Stress has no connection to substance use
Stress is a recognized risk factor that can lead some people toward substance use as an unhealthy coping method
Only physical stress matters, not emotional stress
quiz.e: Unmanaged stress is a documented risk factor that can lead to substance use as maladaptive coping.

quiz.q: Which best reflects a key prevention message about substance use?
o: Using substances once has no long-term risk
Avoiding early use and building healthy coping skills reduces lifetime risk of dependence
Only genetics determine substance use outcomes
quiz.e: Delaying use and building coping/refusal skills are proven strategies to reduce lifetime addiction risk.

quiz.q: Caffeine, in excessive amounts, acts on the body as a:
quiz.e: Caffeine is a stimulant that increases heart rate and alertness, similar to other stimulants in excess.

quiz.q: Puberty is primarily triggered by:
quiz.e: Puberty is triggered by rising levels of hormones like estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone.

quiz.q: Which hormone is primarily responsible for male physical changes during puberty?
quiz.e: Testosterone drives male puberty changes like voice deepening and increased muscle mass.

quiz.q: Which is a typical physical change during female puberty?
quiz.e: The onset of menstruation is a hallmark physical change of female puberty.

quiz.q: At what general age range does puberty typically begin, though it varies?
quiz.e: Puberty typically starts between ages 8-14, with wide, normal individual variation.

quiz.q: Which brain region continues developing into the mid-20s?
quiz.e: The prefrontal cortex, involved in judgment and impulse control, matures into the mid-20s.

quiz.q: Which organ in the female reproductive system produces eggs?
quiz.e: The ovaries produce eggs (ova) as well as key reproductive hormones.

quiz.q: The menstrual cycle is generally about how many days?
quiz.e: The typical menstrual cycle is about 28 days, though it can vary between individuals.

quiz.q: Sperm cells are produced in which male organ?
quiz.e: The testes produce sperm cells as well as testosterone.

quiz.q: Fertilization typically occurs in which location?
quiz.e: Fertilization, when sperm meets egg, typically occurs in the fallopian tube.

quiz.q: Which gland regulates hormones for both reproductive systems?
quiz.e: The pituitary gland in the brain regulates the hormones controlling reproduction.

quiz.q: During which trimester do major organs begin to form?
quiz.e: The first trimester (weeks 1-12) is critical for organ formation, making it sensitive to harmful exposures.

quiz.q: Fetal movement is typically first felt by the mother during which trimester?
quiz.e: Movement is generally felt during the second trimester as the fetus grows and develops.

quiz.q: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs) result from:
quiz.e: FASDs are caused by alcohol exposure during pregnancy and can cause lifelong effects.

quiz.q: Prenatal care refers to:
o: Regular medical checkups during pregnancy to monitor mother and baby's health
quiz.e: Prenatal care involves regular checkups that monitor the health of both mother and developing baby.

quiz.q: Which substance use during pregnancy is linked to serious birth defects?
quiz.e: Alcohol, tobacco, and certain drugs during pregnancy can cause serious developmental harm.

quiz.q: Which STI often causes no symptoms, making testing especially important?
quiz.e: Chlamydia frequently causes no symptoms, so routine testing is important for sexually active people.

quiz.q: Which method is the only one that is 100% effective at preventing both pregnancy and STIs?
quiz.e: Abstinence is the only method with zero risk of pregnancy or STI transmission.

quiz.q: Which vaccine can prevent infection with cancer-linked strains of a common STI?
quiz.e: The HPV vaccine prevents infection with HPV strains linked to cervical and other cancers.

quiz.q: Untreated STIs can lead to which serious complication?
quiz.e: Untreated STIs, especially chlamydia and gonorrhea, can cause infertility.

quiz.q: Which is true about condoms and STI prevention?
o: They eliminate all STI risk completely
When used correctly and consistently, they significantly reduce (but don't eliminate) STI risk
They have no effect on STI transmission
They only prevent pregnancy, never STIs
quiz.e: Condoms greatly reduce STI transmission risk when used correctly, but are not 100% effective.

quiz.q: Hormonal birth control methods work primarily by:
quiz.e: Hormonal methods like the pill work by regulating hormones to prevent ovulation.

quiz.q: Which statement about contraception effectiveness is accurate?
o: All methods except abstinence carry some risk of pregnancy
quiz.e: Every method other than abstinence carries some statistical risk of pregnancy.

quiz.q: Responsible decision-making about sexual activity should include considering:
o: Physical, emotional, legal, and future-goal consequences
quiz.e: Responsible decisions weigh physical, emotional, legal, and long-term goal impacts.

quiz.q: According to Erikson's stages, adolescence is primarily focused on:
quiz.e: Erikson identifies adolescence as centered on developing a stable sense of identity.

quiz.q: Which best reflects readiness for responsible parenting?
o: Emotional maturity, financial stability, and a strong support system
Being any age with no other requirements
Wanting a baby is the only requirement
quiz.e: Responsible parenting requires emotional maturity, financial stability, and support systems most teens lack.

quiz.q: Teen pregnancy is associated with:
o: Increased health risks for parent and baby, plus social and financial challenges
Decreased health risks compared to adult pregnancy
quiz.e: Teen pregnancy carries higher health risks and significant social/financial challenges.

quiz.q: Healthy family relationships are built on:
quiz.e: Strong families rely on open communication, mutual respect, and shared responsibility.

quiz.q: Which life stage follows adolescence in typical developmental sequence?
quiz.e: Adulthood follows adolescence in the typical human life stage sequence.

quiz.q: Which is an emotional change commonly associated with puberty?
quiz.e: Hormonal shifts during puberty commonly cause mood swings and heightened self-consciousness.

quiz.q: HIV is different from many other STIs because it:
o: Is a lifelong viral condition with no cure, though manageable with treatment
Cannot be prevented in any way
quiz.e: HIV is a lifelong condition managed with treatment, but currently has no cure.

quiz.q: Which best describes the second trimester of pregnancy?
o: Weeks 13-27, rapid growth and often felt movement
It doesn't exist in a typical pregnancy
quiz.e: The second trimester (weeks 13-27) involves rapid growth, with movement often felt by the mother.

quiz.q: Which best describes the third trimester of pregnancy?
o: Continued growth and organ maturation preparing for birth
quiz.e: The third trimester focuses on continued growth and maturation in preparation for birth.

quiz.q: A key reason abstinence education emphasizes decision-making skills is:
o: To eliminate the need for any health education
Because responsible choices reduce risks of pregnancy, STIs, and emotional harm
Because it's the only topic in health class
Because decision-making has no connection to sexual health
quiz.e: Strong decision-making skills help reduce risks associated with early or unprotected sexual activity.

quiz.q: Which best explains why regular STI testing matters even without symptoms?
o: Testing is only needed if symptoms appear
Many STIs are asymptomatic, so testing is the only reliable way to detect them
Only certain age groups need testing
quiz.e: Because many STIs show no symptoms, routine testing is essential for early detection.

quiz.q: Which describes the role of the epididymis in the male reproductive system?
o: It is part of the female anatomy
quiz.e: The epididymis stores and helps mature sperm cells before ejaculation.

quiz.q: Which best reflects a healthy approach to discussing reproductive health questions?
o: Talking with a trusted adult or healthcare provider for accurate information
Relying only on unverified social media claims
Avoiding the topic entirely leads to better outcomes
quiz.e: Trusted adults and healthcare providers provide accurate, reliable reproductive health information.

quiz.q: Which best summarizes why understanding puberty timing variation matters?
o: Everyone should worry if they develop differently from friends
Normal puberty timing varies widely, so different timing isn't a cause for concern
Puberty must occur at the exact same time for all people
Variation in timing indicates a health problem
quiz.e: Wide normal variation in puberty timing means different timelines are not inherently concerning.

quiz.q: Which best describes ovulation?
o: The shedding of the uterine lining
The release of an egg from the ovary
quiz.e: Ovulation is the release of a mature egg from the ovary, roughly at the midpoint of the cycle.

quiz.q: Which best reflects the purpose of learning about life stages in health class?
o: To memorize ages with no practical use
To understand developmental tasks and build realistic expectations across the lifespan
Life stages have no educational value
quiz.e: Understanding life stages helps build realistic expectations about physical and social development over time.

quiz.q: Which best describes the vas deferens in the male reproductive system?
o: A tube that transports sperm from the epididymis toward the urethra
Part of the female reproductive anatomy
quiz.e: The vas deferens carries mature sperm from the epididymis toward the urethra during ejaculation.

quiz.q: What does the 'C' in RICE stand for when treating a sprain?
quiz.e: RICE = Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a sprain and a strain?
o: A sprain injures a ligament; a strain injures a muscle or tendon
A sprain injures a muscle; a strain injures a ligament
A sprain is always more serious than a strain
quiz.e: Ligaments connect bone to bone (sprain); muscles/tendons connect muscle to bone (strain).

quiz.q: Why should ice never be applied directly to bare skin?
o: It can cause frostbite with prolonged contact
It numbs the pain too much
quiz.e: A cloth barrier prevents frostbite while still reducing swelling.

quiz.q: A teammate twists their ankle and can't bear weight on it. What should you suspect and do?
o: A possible fracture — immobilize it and seek medical care
A sprain only — walk it off
quiz.e: Inability to bear weight is a fracture warning sign; immobilize rather than move or straighten it.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't you move someone with a suspected spinal injury unless there's immediate danger?
o: It makes the injury heal slower
quiz.e: Unnecessary movement of a suspected spinal injury can cause further, sometimes permanent, damage.

quiz.q: When is applying heat (instead of ice) appropriate for a soft-tissue injury?
o: After the first 48 hours, for stiffness
quiz.e: Heat early on increases swelling; it's better used later for lingering stiffness.

quiz.q: What is the correct compression rate for hands-only CPR on an adult?
quiz.e: 100-120 compressions per minute is the standard rate for adult CPR.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the Cardiac Chain of Survival?
quiz.e: Recognizing the emergency and calling 911 comes first, before CPR and defibrillation can begin.

quiz.q: How does an AED decide whether to deliver a shock?
o: It analyzes the heart's rhythm and only shocks a shockable rhythm
The user must decide when to shock
quiz.e: AEDs are designed to be safe for untrained bystanders because they analyze rhythm first.

quiz.q: What technique is used to help a choking adult who cannot cough, speak, or breathe?
o: Back slaps only, never abdominal thrusts
quiz.e: Abdominal thrusts are the standard first response for a conscious, choking adult.

quiz.q: About how quickly can brain damage begin from lack of oxygen during cardiac arrest?
o: Brain damage cannot occur from this
quiz.e: This narrow window is why immediate 911 calls and CPR matter so much.

quiz.q: What do Good Samaritan laws generally do?
o: Protect bystanders who give reasonable emergency help in good faith from being sued
Require everyone to be certified in CPR
Make it illegal not to help someone
quiz.e: These laws encourage bystanders to help without fear of legal liability for honest mistakes.

quiz.q: Why is texting while driving with a hands-free setup still risky?
o: It still diverts cognitive attention from driving
It isn't risky at all if hands-free
It only affects reaction time at night
quiz.e: Cognitive distraction, not just physical distraction, slows reaction time significantly.

quiz.q: Roughly how much does wearing a seatbelt reduce the risk of fatal injury in a crash?
quiz.e: Seatbelts cut fatal injury risk by roughly half in most crash scenarios.

quiz.q: Why do graduated driver's licensing (GDL) programs restrict nighttime driving and passenger numbers for new teen drivers?
o: Both factors significantly raise crash risk for new drivers
Because cars run less safely at night
quiz.e: Inexperience combined with nighttime conditions or passenger distraction raises crash risk substantially.

quiz.q: What should a pedestrian do to cross a street safely?
o: Cross at marked crosswalks and make eye contact with drivers
quiz.e: Crosswalks and driver eye contact both reduce pedestrian risk.

quiz.q: Why is silent, fast drowning more dangerous than the 'movie version' of drowning?
o: It often doesn't look like an emergency, so it can go unnoticed
It never actually happens in real life
quiz.e: Real drowning is often quiet and quick, which is why constant supervision near water is critical.

quiz.q: What is the most effective way to prevent drowning while boating?
o: Wearing a properly fitted life jacket
quiz.e: A life jacket protects even strong swimmers who may be injured, exhausted, or in cold water.

quiz.q: What distinguishes heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
o: Heat stroke involves hot, dry skin and confusion and is a medical emergency
Heat stroke is always milder than heat exhaustion
Heat exhaustion requires calling 911 immediately, heat stroke does not
quiz.e: Heat stroke is more severe, with the body unable to cool itself, and requires immediate emergency care.

quiz.q: During a lightning storm, what is the safest place to be?
o: Indoors or in a hard-topped vehicle
quiz.e: Open areas, tall trees, and water are all high-risk locations during lightning.

quiz.q: What defines bullying, distinguishing it from a normal disagreement?
o: A repeated, intentional imbalance of power
quiz.e: Bullying involves repetition and a power imbalance, not just conflict.

quiz.q: How do bystanders most effectively reduce the duration of bullying?
o: By speaking up, supporting the target, or reporting it to an adult
By recording it for social media
By joining in to avoid becoming a target
quiz.e: Bystander intervention and adult reporting are shown to shorten bullying incidents.

quiz.q: Which strategy helps de-escalate a tense conflict?
o: Staying calm, using a non-threatening tone, and giving space
Raising your voice to assert dominance
Standing very close to the other person
quiz.e: Calm tone, space, and non-confrontational body language reduce escalation.

quiz.q: What is a key firearm safety practice for reducing unintentional injury and suicide risk in a home?
o: Storing firearms unloaded and separate from ammunition
Keeping firearms loaded for quick access
There is no effective safety practice
Storing ammunition next to the firearm
quiz.e: Safe, separated storage significantly reduces both unintentional injury and suicide risk.

quiz.q: What is an important feature of a home fire escape plan?
o: Two ways out of every room and a designated meeting spot
A plan is unnecessary if smoke detectors exist
Escape plans should never be practiced
quiz.e: Multiple exits and a meeting spot, practiced regularly, save lives since fatal fires often occur at night.

quiz.q: What is the correct first action when calling 911 for an emergency?
o: Stay calm, state your exact location, and answer the dispatcher's questions
Hang up immediately after stating the problem
Only call if you're certain it's serious
Give your name before your location
quiz.e: Location is the most urgent information a dispatcher needs to send help.

quiz.q: Why are universal precautions like wearing gloves important when helping an injured person?
o: They protect both the helper and the injured person from infection
They are only for use in hospitals
They aren't necessary for minor injuries
They slow down the response time unnecessarily
quiz.e: Avoiding contact with blood and bodily fluids reduces infection risk for both parties.

quiz.q: What items belong in a basic first aid kit?
o: Bandages, gauze, antiseptic, tape, and gloves
quiz.e: A functional first aid kit includes basic wound care supplies plus any needed personal medication.

quiz.q: What is the 'check, call, care' model used for?
o: A basic framework for responding to any emergency
A rule for scheduling doctor visits
A step used only by paramedics
quiz.e: Check the scene for danger, call 911, then provide care you're trained to give.

quiz.q: Why should a disaster preparedness plan be specific to your region?
o: Different regions face different risks, like earthquakes vs. hurricanes
All disasters require the same exact plan
Regional plans are only for emergency workers
Disaster plans are not useful for families
quiz.e: Preparedness should match the likely hazards of your specific location.

quiz.q: A cyclist can reduce the risk of serious head injury most by:
quiz.e: Helmets are proven to significantly reduce serious head injury risk in a crash.

quiz.q: Which best describes hypothermia?
o: Dangerously low body temperature causing shivering and confusion
The same condition as heat stroke
quiz.e: Hypothermia results from cold exposure and can become life-threatening as it worsens.

quiz.q: What should you do if you notice warning signs that a friend may be at risk for violence, like talk of hurting themselves?
o: Tell a trusted adult right away
Keep it a secret to respect their privacy
Wait to see if it happens again
quiz.e: Warning signs should always be reported to a trusted adult, not kept secret.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign that requires immediate emergency medical attention after alcohol consumption?
o: Vomiting while unconscious and slowed breathing
Wanting to lie down for a while
quiz.e: These are signs of alcohol poisoning, a medical emergency requiring immediate help.

quiz.q: Why is DUI (driving under the influence) especially dangerous?
o: It impairs judgment, reaction time, and coordination all at once
It has no measurable effect on driving
It only matters at very high speeds
quiz.e: Alcohol and drugs impair multiple driving-critical skills simultaneously.

quiz.q: What is the best response if a fire alarm goes off in a building?
o: Follow your practiced escape route and exit calmly
Use the elevator to leave faster
Wait to see if it's a real fire
quiz.e: Following a practiced escape route without delay is the safest response.

quiz.q: Which of these is a de-escalation technique for a heated argument?
o: Taking a short break and returning to the conversation calmly
Bringing in more people to take sides
quiz.e: A cooling-off period prevents conflicts from escalating further.

quiz.q: What is the main reason children and teens are at higher risk in car crashes without proper restraints?
o: Restraints like seatbelts and car seats are proven to reduce fatal injury
Age has no effect on crash risk
Restraints are only useful for adults
Younger passengers are naturally safer unrestrained
quiz.e: Proper restraint use is one of the most effective ways to reduce injury risk at any age.

quiz.q: When should you NOT try to realign or straighten a suspected broken bone?
o: Always — immobilize it as found instead
Only if it's a leg fracture
quiz.e: Realigning a fracture without training can cause further damage; immobilization is correct first aid.

quiz.q: What is one reason lifeguard-supervised swim areas are safer than unsupervised open water?
o: Trained lifeguards can spot and respond to distress quickly
Supervised areas have no risk at all
Lifeguards are only for young children
quiz.e: Quick recognition and response to distress in water significantly improves survival odds.

quiz.q: What makes a disease 'communicable'?
o: It is caused by a pathogen and can spread between people
It only affects one person and never spreads
quiz.e: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens that can be transmitted person to person.

quiz.q: Which of these is a noncommunicable disease?
quiz.e: Type 2 diabetes is not spread person to person; it's linked to genetics, lifestyle, and environment.

quiz.q: What distinguishes an acute disease from a chronic disease?
o: Acute comes on quickly and resolves; chronic persists over a long time
quiz.e: Acute illness (like a cold) is short-term; chronic illness (like heart disease) persists long-term.

quiz.q: What is the difference between an epidemic and a pandemic?
o: An epidemic is localized rapid spread; a pandemic is a global outbreak
They mean exactly the same thing
A pandemic is always less severe
An epidemic only applies to animals
quiz.e: Scale is the key difference — epidemic is regional, pandemic is global.

quiz.q: How can a disease with an infectious cause still have a chronic, noncommunicable course?
o: Like HPV-linked cancers, which develop long after the initial infection
Chronic diseases cannot have infectious origins
quiz.e: HPV is infectious, but the cancers it can cause develop chronically over time.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the body's first line of defense against pathogens?
o: Physical barriers like skin and mucous membranes
quiz.e: Skin and mucous membranes physically block pathogens before they enter the body.

quiz.q: What is the main job of an antibody?
o: Recognize and bind to a specific pathogen to mark it for destruction
quiz.e: Antibodies target specific pathogens as part of the immune response.

quiz.q: Why can the body respond faster to a pathogen it has encountered before?
o: Memory cells remain after the first infection
quiz.e: Memory cells allow a quicker, stronger immune response upon re-exposure.

quiz.q: Why is a fever often actually a helpful immune response?
o: Higher body temperature makes conditions less favorable for many pathogens
Fever always indicates a dangerous illness
Fever is caused only by bacteria
quiz.e: Elevated temperature can slow pathogen reproduction, aiding the immune response.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common route of pathogen transmission?
o: Respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing
quiz.e: Respiratory droplets are a major transmission route for illnesses like the flu and colds.

quiz.q: How does a vaccine train the immune system?
o: By introducing a weakened, inactivated, or partial pathogen so the body builds memory cells
By curing an active infection instantly
By eliminating the need for an immune system
quiz.e: Vaccines create immune memory without causing the actual disease.

quiz.q: What is herd immunity?
o: Protection that occurs when enough of a population is immune, slowing disease spread
A vaccine given only to farm animals
Immunity that lasts only one day
A myth with no scientific basis
quiz.e: High vaccination rates protect vulnerable people who can't be vaccinated themselves.

quiz.q: Why can declining vaccination rates allow diseases like measles to reemerge?
o: Herd immunity weakens, allowing the pathogen to spread more easily
Vaccines become less effective with fewer people using them
quiz.e: Lower vaccination coverage reduces herd immunity, enabling outbreaks.

quiz.q: What are mild side effects like soreness or low fever after a vaccine a sign of?
o: The immune system responding as expected, not illness
quiz.e: These mild effects show the immune system is building protection, not causing sickness.

quiz.q: What causes atherosclerosis?
o: A buildup of plaque that narrows arteries
quiz.e: Atherosclerosis is plaque buildup that narrows and stiffens arteries, raising cardiovascular risk.

quiz.q: Which of these is a modifiable cardiovascular risk factor?
quiz.e: Smoking is a lifestyle factor a person can change, unlike age or genetics.

quiz.q: Why does having no known risk factors not guarantee someone won't develop a disease?
o: Risk factors change probability, not certainty
quiz.e: Risk factors shift likelihood but don't remove or guarantee outcomes.

quiz.q: What is the value of regular cancer screenings like skin checks or Pap tests?
o: They allow many cancers to be caught early, when treatment is most effective
They prevent cancer from ever occurring
They are only useful after symptoms appear
They replace the need for a healthy lifestyle
quiz.e: Early detection through screening greatly improves treatment outcomes.

quiz.q: Which lifestyle factor is most linked to preventing or delaying type 2 diabetes?
o: Regular physical activity and maintaining a healthy weight
Sleeping less than 5 hours a night
quiz.e: Physical activity and weight management are strongly linked to type 2 diabetes prevention.

quiz.q: How is type 2 diabetes different from type 1 diabetes in terms of prevention?
o: Type 2 is strongly linked to lifestyle and can often be delayed or prevented
Type 1 is fully preventable through diet
Both are equally preventable through lifestyle
Neither type has any lifestyle connection
quiz.e: Type 1 is an autoimmune condition, while type 2 has strong lifestyle links.

quiz.q: Which habit reduces risk for multiple chronic diseases at once?
quiz.e: Avoiding tobacco/vaping reduces risk of cancer, heart disease, and lung disease simultaneously.

quiz.q: Why do routine checkups help prevent chronic disease?
o: They can catch early warning signs like rising blood pressure before a disease develops
They are only useful once a disease is diagnosed
They replace the need for healthy habits
They have no real preventive value
quiz.e: Regular monitoring allows early intervention before conditions become full diagnoses.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap to effectively reduce illness spread?
o: Only until visible dirt is gone
quiz.e: 20 seconds is the recommended minimum for effective handwashing.

quiz.q: Why should you cough or sneeze into your elbow rather than your hands?
o: It reduces spreading respiratory droplets to surfaces you touch
quiz.e: Using the elbow keeps hands cleaner, reducing pathogen transfer to surfaces and other people.

quiz.q: Why is staying home when sick with a contagious illness important?
o: It protects others, especially those at higher risk
It has no effect on community spread
It only matters for serious illnesses
Sick days always make illness worse
quiz.e: Staying home reduces exposure for vulnerable people like infants and immunocompromised individuals.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of foodborne illness that proper cooking temperatures prevent?
o: Bacteria like Salmonella and E. coli
quiz.e: Cooking food to safe temperatures kills harmful bacteria that cause foodborne illness.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't you share water bottles or utensils with others?
o: Pathogens that live in saliva can spread this way
Sharing items has no health impact
It's only a concern for adults
quiz.e: Saliva can carry pathogens, so sharing personal items increases transmission risk.

quiz.q: Do antibiotics work against viral illnesses like the common cold?
o: No — antibiotics only treat bacterial infections
quiz.e: Antibiotics are ineffective against viruses; they target bacteria specifically.

quiz.q: Can a person spread a communicable illness before showing symptoms?
o: Yes, during an incubation period before symptoms appear
No, symptoms always appear before contagion begins
Only children can spread illness without symptoms
This is impossible for any illness
quiz.e: Many pathogens are contagious during an asymptomatic incubation period.

quiz.q: Which government agency is most responsible for regulating vaccine and drug safety in the U.S.?
quiz.e: The FDA regulates the safety and approval of drugs and vaccines.

quiz.q: What does 'B vitamins help convert food into usable energy' describe?
o: A micronutrient function related to metabolism, not disease prevention directly
A description of a communicable disease
quiz.e: This links back to metabolism, distinct from the immune/disease-prevention concepts of this unit.

quiz.q: Which best explains why disinfecting frequently touched surfaces reduces illness?
o: Pathogens can survive outside the body on surfaces for a time
quiz.e: Many pathogens can survive on surfaces, so cleaning reduces transmission opportunities.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between smoking and disease risk?
o: Smoking raises risk of cancer, heart disease, and lung disease simultaneously
Smoking has no proven health effects
Smoking only matters for older adults
quiz.e: Tobacco use is one of the most significant modifiable risk factors across multiple chronic diseases.

quiz.q: Why might a community experience a measles outbreak despite the disease being previously rare?
o: A drop in local vaccination rates reduced herd immunity
Measles cannot be prevented by vaccination
Outbreaks are always random and unrelated to vaccination
Herd immunity does not apply to measles
quiz.e: Herd immunity gaps from declining vaccination allow contagious diseases to reemerge.

quiz.q: What best describes the immune system's white blood cells?
o: They engulf pathogens and help produce targeted antibodies
They are the body's only defense mechanism
They only function during a fever
quiz.e: White blood cells are central to the body's second and third lines of immune defense.

quiz.q: Which of these best supports overall chronic disease prevention?
o: A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains
A diet high in processed foods and added sugar
quiz.e: A nutrient-dense diet lowers risk across multiple chronic conditions.

quiz.q: What is a practical reason family health history matters even with healthy habits?
o: Non-modifiable risk factors like genetics still influence disease risk
Genetics have no influence on disease risk
Family history only matters for rare diseases
Healthy habits eliminate all genetic risk
quiz.e: Genetics is a non-modifiable factor that combines with lifestyle to determine overall risk.

quiz.q: Which best summarizes how vector-borne disease spreads?
o: Through a carrier like a mosquito or tick that transmits a pathogen
quiz.e: Vectors like mosquitoes and ticks physically transmit certain pathogens between hosts.

quiz.q: Why are memory cells important after recovering from a communicable illness?
o: They allow the immune system to respond faster if exposed again
They cause the same illness to recur
They only exist in early childhood
quiz.e: Memory cells are the basis for long-term immunity after infection or vaccination.

quiz.q: What is the primary goal of public health disease surveillance?
o: Detecting health trends early to allow a faster response
Only tracking disease after an outbreak ends
quiz.e: Ongoing surveillance allows earlier, more effective public health responses to emerging threats.

quiz.q: What is health fraud (quackery)?
o: Selling products or services with false or exaggerated health claims
A government program to test new drugs
A type of health insurance plan
quiz.e: Quackery preys on people seeking quick fixes with unproven or false claims.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag that a health product might be a scam?
o: Claims of a 'miracle cure' suppressed by doctors
FDA approval listed on the label
quiz.e: Claims of suppression by 'the establishment' are a classic manipulation tactic.

quiz.q: What advertising technique relies on 'everyone is using it' messaging?
quiz.e: Bandwagon appeals pressure consumers through perceived popularity, not evidence.

quiz.q: Before acting on a health claim, what's a smart critical-consumer step?
o: Check it against a credible source like a doctor or peer-reviewed study
Trust it if it has a celebrity endorsement
Assume any online claim is accurate
Buy it immediately if it's on sale
quiz.e: Verifying claims against credible sources is the core critical-consumer skill.

quiz.q: How strictly does the FDA regulate dietary supplements compared to medications?
o: Supplements aren't regulated by any agency
quiz.e: Supplements face much lighter FDA regulation than prescription or OTC drugs.

quiz.q: What is a health insurance premium?
o: The regular amount paid for insurance regardless of care used
A one-time fee paid only during a hospital visit
The total cost of a single prescription
quiz.e: A premium is paid on a regular schedule (often monthly) to maintain coverage.

quiz.q: What is a deductible?
o: The amount paid out-of-pocket before insurance starts covering its share
The same thing as a premium
A fee only for emergency visits
A refund from an insurance company
quiz.e: Once the deductible is met, insurance begins paying its portion of covered costs.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a copay and coinsurance?
o: A copay is a fixed fee; coinsurance is a percentage of the cost
Coinsurance is always more expensive than copay
Copay only applies to emergency care
quiz.e: Copay = flat fee; coinsurance = percentage split of cost.

quiz.q: Why is preventive care often covered at no additional cost by insurance plans?
o: It catches problems early and reduces long-term costs
Preventive care has no real medical value
Insurance companies are required to lose money on it
It only applies to people over 65
quiz.e: Early detection through preventive care saves money and improves outcomes long-term.

quiz.q: Why is an ER visit generally far more expensive than urgent care?
o: ERs are equipped and staffed for life-threatening emergencies, driving higher costs
Cost has nothing to do with the type of facility
quiz.e: ER-level staffing and equipment come at a much higher cost than urgent care.

quiz.q: What can happen when someone is uninsured or underinsured?
o: They may delay care, letting conditions become more serious and costly
They automatically receive free care everywhere
They are legally barred from seeing a doctor
quiz.e: Delayed care due to cost often worsens conditions and raises eventual treatment costs.

quiz.q: What does a primary care provider typically manage?
o: Overall health, routine checkups, and referrals to specialists
quiz.e: Primary care providers coordinate general health and refer patients to specialists as needed.

quiz.q: When is a specialist typically needed?
o: For a specific body system or condition beyond general primary care
quiz.e: Specialists focus on specific conditions and often require a referral.

quiz.q: What kind of issue is urgent care best suited for?
o: Non-life-threatening issues needing prompt attention, like a minor infection
quiz.e: Urgent care fills the gap between routine care and the emergency room.

quiz.q: Which mental health provider can prescribe medication?
o: No mental health provider can prescribe medication
quiz.e: Psychiatrists are medical doctors who can prescribe psychiatric medication.

quiz.q: What is telehealth most useful for?
o: Virtual appointments like follow-ups or mental health visits
quiz.e: Telehealth expands access for many, but isn't appropriate for every medical situation.

quiz.q: What is the main role of the CDC?
o: Tracking disease outbreaks and issuing public health guidance in the U.S.
quiz.e: The CDC focuses on national disease tracking, research, and health guidance.

quiz.q: What does the FDA regulate?
o: Safety of food, drugs, vaccines, and medical devices
quiz.e: The FDA's core role is regulating safety and labeling of food, drugs, and devices.

quiz.q: What can the WHO do in response to a serious global disease outbreak?
o: Declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern
Directly pass laws in individual countries
quiz.e: The WHO coordinates and can formally declare global-level health emergencies.

quiz.q: Which of these is typically handled by local or state health departments?
quiz.e: Local/state health departments manage community-level public health services.

quiz.q: What does the EPA primarily regulate that affects community health?
quiz.e: The EPA sets and enforces environmental quality standards that impact public health.

quiz.q: How does air pollution commonly affect community health?
o: It's linked to asthma and cardiovascular disease
It has no measurable health effects
quiz.e: Air pollution from vehicles and industry is linked to multiple chronic conditions.

quiz.q: What is a 'food desert'?
o: An area with limited access to affordable, healthy food
A dry climate region with no farming
A neighborhood with too many grocery stores
quiz.e: Food deserts are linked to poorer diet quality and higher chronic disease rates.

quiz.q: What does environmental justice recognize?
o: Pollution and health hazards are often unevenly distributed, hurting lower-income communities most
All communities face identical environmental risks
Wealthier communities always face more pollution
quiz.e: Environmental justice highlights inequities in who bears the burden of pollution.

quiz.q: How does access to parks and sidewalks affect community health?
o: It affects how much physical activity residents can realistically get
It has no connection to physical activity levels
Only rural areas benefit from parks
Sidewalks only matter for safety, not health
quiz.e: Safe, accessible recreational spaces support more physical activity in a community.

quiz.q: What is one example of a community health resource that fills care gaps?
o: A free clinic or school-based health center
quiz.e: Free clinics and school-based centers provide access for underserved populations.

quiz.q: What is an example of policy-level health advocacy?
o: Supporting a public health law, like a clean air regulation
Asking a doctor a question during a visit
quiz.e: Policy-level advocacy involves supporting laws and regulations that affect public health broadly.

quiz.q: What makes health messaging campaigns effective at changing community behavior?
o: Clear calls to action and relatable messengers
quiz.e: Effective campaigns are clear, actionable, and delivered by trusted messengers.

quiz.q: What is peer health education?
o: Trained students teaching other students accurate health information
quiz.e: Peer education leverages trusted peer relationships to spread accurate health information.

quiz.q: What makes someone a credible health advocate?
o: Using accurate, current information from reliable sources
Sharing whatever is trending on social media
quiz.e: Credibility in advocacy depends on accurate, well-sourced information.

quiz.q: How is voting connected to public health?
o: Many policies, like clean air rules, directly affect public health
Voting has no connection to health outcomes
Only healthcare workers should vote on health issues
quiz.e: Civic engagement, including voting, shapes policies with direct health impacts.

quiz.q: Why should you compare ingredients and independent reviews rather than packaging when buying a health product?
o: Packaging and celebrity endorsement don't guarantee quality or effectiveness
Packaging is the most reliable indicator of quality
Ingredients don't matter for health products
quiz.e: Evidence-based comparison leads to better consumer decisions than marketing alone.

quiz.q: Which best describes coinsurance?
o: A percentage of a medical cost shared between patient and insurer
A fixed dollar amount per visit
The total yearly cost of insurance
A penalty for missing a payment
quiz.e: Coinsurance splits cost by percentage, unlike a copay's fixed fee.

quiz.q: Why might checking if a provider is 'in-network' matter before choosing care?
o: Out-of-network care often costs significantly more under an insurance plan
Network status has no effect on cost
All providers charge the same rate
In-network providers are always worse quality
quiz.e: Insurance plans typically cover in-network care at a lower cost to the patient.

quiz.q: What is one practical benefit of telehealth for mental health care?
o: It has expanded access, especially for follow-up and counseling visits
It replaces the need for any in-person mental health care
It only works for physical injuries
It's not covered by any insurance
quiz.e: Telehealth has notably increased access to mental health follow-up care.

quiz.q: Which government level is most responsible for enforcing local restaurant food safety inspections?
quiz.e: Restaurant inspections are typically a local/state health department responsibility.

quiz.q: What should a critical consumer do when a product claims 'doctors don't want you to know this'?
o: Treat it as a red flag for a possible scam
Trust it immediately since doctors are mentioned
Buy it right away before it sells out
Assume it must be true if it sounds scientific
quiz.e: Claims of suppressed information are a hallmark of health fraud messaging.

quiz.q: Why do many public health agencies rely heavily on data surveillance?
o: To detect health trends early and respond faster
Because it's required for insurance purposes only
Surveillance data is not actually useful
To replace the need for hospitals
quiz.e: Ongoing data collection allows agencies to catch and respond to emerging health issues early.

quiz.q: What is an appropriate use of an emergency room versus urgent care?
o: ER for life-threatening conditions; urgent care for prompt but non-life-threatening needs
ER for all illnesses, urgent care for nothing
Urgent care for life-threatening conditions only
There's no meaningful difference in appropriate use
quiz.e: Matching the facility to the severity of the condition saves money and gets more appropriate care.

quiz.q: Why does the FDA's lighter regulation of supplements matter to consumers?
o: Supplement claims and safety are less rigorously verified before reaching shelves
It means supplements are always dangerous
It means supplements are more effective than drugs
It has no practical impact on consumers
quiz.e: Consumers should be more critical of supplement claims given lighter regulatory oversight.
